text: Only two people shared her special seat, a fine old man in a velvet coat and a big old woman with a roll of knitting on her apron. <break time="0.8s" /> They did not speak, which was rather disappointing, for Miss Brill always looked forward to the conversation every Sunday. <break time="0.8s" /> She had become quite expert, she thought, at listening as though she did not listen, at sitting in other peoples lives just for a minute while they talked around her. <break time="0.8s" /> Last Sunday an Englishman in a dreadful Panama hat and his wife in button boots had sat there, and the wife had talked the whole time about spectacles. <break time="0.8s" /> She knew she needed them, but nothing her patient husband suggested could please her, and Miss Brill had wanted to shake her. <break time="0.8s" /> Now she watched the crowd, the couples and groups who were strolling to and fro, stopping to talk, to greet, and to buy flowers from an old beggar. <break time="0.8s" /> Little children ran among them, swooping and laughing, and when one small child suddenly fell down, its mother rushed to the rescue like a young hen. <break time="0.8s" /> Other people sat on the benches, but they were odd, silent, and nearly all old, as if they had just come from dark little rooms or even cupboards.
